source.title: Reinforced stochastic gradient descent for deep neural network learning

record.file_problem: none; supplied text is the full paper, though some equations and figure text are garbled in extraction
record.tranche_reason: Tests how a new optimizer changes training and held-out error on synthetic data and MNIST, comparing with standard gradient methods and adaptive optimizers; this is a new optimizer setting for the generalization claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own training and test errors under R-SGD and comparator optimizers. The references to other studies are not recorded as results. Values available only in plots are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The MNIST experiments report Adam and vanilla minibatch SGD (BackProp) held-out errors under limited tuning, directly bearing on V4. Adam substantially outperforms vanilla SGD. Comparisons involving the proposed R-SGD method alone do not establish the claimed adaptive-versus-standard-SGD difference.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that R-SGD performs comparably to Adam on MNIST and better on their synthetic task while requiring less gradient-state memory. They attribute its performance to stochastic reuse of previous gradients and leave more complex architectures and datasets for future study.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces reinforced SGD, which stochastically accumulates previous gradients; compares with BackProp, Adam, and momentum variants. The work does not test random-label memorization or the original claim's experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with reinforcement schedule (γ0, λ); MNIST performs better with Γ(t) = 1 − 1/√(t + 1) than the synthetic-task schedule. Training data size changes the R-SGD versus Adam comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: R-SGD reduces synthetic-regression test error relative to BackProp and Adam, despite higher training error than Adam.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic reinforcement of gradients can improve held-out regression performance relative to these optimizer settings.

fits_no_version.finding: R-SGD matches Adam's mean MNIST error at 10K examples and has a slightly lower mean at 15K.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed nonadaptive R-SGD method can achieve MNIST performance comparable to Adam.

fits_no_version.finding: R-SGD compares favorably with several fixed or scheduled momentum methods; adaptive-momentum SGDM performs similarly on the synthetic task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic gradient accumulation can match or improve on deterministic momentum in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Bilinear interpolation produces a sharper-looking test-error subspace for R-SGD than Adam, although their solutions have similar quality.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visual sharpness of interpolated test-error surfaces need not distinguish optimizer solution quality.

record.problems: The main task is synthetic continuous-label regression and MNIST classification, with small fully connected networks; no random labels or memorization-capacity check. Some comparisons and trajectories are only shown in figures, and exact values are unavailable in the supplied extraction. Authors state more complex models and datasets remain for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results were left out. Row R13 was not a distinct intervention result and is omitted from valid extracted rows; the text says adaptive-momentum SGDM can reach similar performance to R-SGD on the toy task, but provides no separate numeric result. Figure-only values are retained as figure-only rather than reconstructed.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error.
Language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and whether Adam has equal or better training performance in the tabulated MNIST comparisons.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations to large-batch training.
Magnitude-scaled perturbations, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.

record.verdict_notes: BackProp is explicitly defined as vanilla minibatch SGD. Adam uses mostly recommended hyperparameters with a modified learning rate; this is not an exhaustive tuning comparison. The challenges apply to the tested MNIST settings and do not refute V4's frequency qualifier across benchmarks. Optimizer names in the record are methods, not model identities.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural and random labels.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
No broad hyperparameter-tuning comparison; only the reported R-SGD, BackProp, Adam, and momentum method settings.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or norm/margin measure.
No example influence or removal experiment.

rows.subject: R-SGD

rows.value: about 77.5% improvement over BackProp, as reported
rows.note: The reported improvement is a relative reduction; the exact test-error values are shown only in the figure. The synthetic task uses continuous target labels.
rows.check: Synthetic continuous-target regression is outside V4's image-classification and language benchmarks. This is a performance comparison of the proposed method with vanilla SGD.
